content:
GTA 6 came out in certain parts of the world this morning, and I've taken the opportunity to dive in and see how the game holds up on all four of the current-generation consoles.

Over the last few hours I've played through the first 30 minutes or so on the Xbox Series S, Xbox Series X, PlayStation 5 and the PlayStation 5 Pro, and largely, the game runs fine no matter which version you're playing. But, that doesn't mean there aren't differences between each of them.

The elephant in the room with all of the machines is the frame rate. That's not surprising, Rockstar came out and told us that the game would be "targeting" 30 fps on all the consoles. But what was surprising is how different that 30 fps feels depending on what you're playing it on.

The biggest example of this is obviously the Xbox Series S. Throughout the prologue and the first part of the first chapter, GTA 6 sits at a pretty steady 30fps, but there are occasionally dips as low as 24fps. Even outside of those super-low dips, turning the camera can sometimes cause the frame rate to jitter a little bit, and while the fps only drops to 27 or 28 in these scenarios, it results in movement that feels like it's dragging on something.

On the base PS5 and Xbox Series X, however, the frame rate stays pretty much locked at 30fps, with only occasional dips to the 27-29 fps range. Keep in mind, though, that I've only got through the first mission, and there is going to be some chaos later in the game that's likely going to wreak more havoc on the 6-year-old CPU in any of the consoles. I know that Digital Foundry has already found a couple of instances on the base PS5, for example. I just don't have the explosives to make that happen yet.

The PS5 Pro is, unsurprisingly, the best way to play GTA 6, and at least in my time with the game so far, it's the version of the game I'd recommend for most people who have the budget to support it. Rockstar's implementation of PSSR really cleans up the presentation, and the ray traced shadows are a godsend in some of the darker scenes I've seen so far. It's also the smoothest version of the game, and I didn't see any dips like I have on all of the other consoles.

It's worth keeping in mind, though, that if you want to buy a PS5 Pro right now, you're basically stuck paying more than $1,400 for the privilege. I don't know if it's worth paying that much, when you can literally save half of that purchasing cost, and the only thing you're really losing out on is better shadows and a couple of frame drops.

Even if you only have the cash for the Xbox Series S, the game still plays fine. You'll get more frame dips, and you'll have to deal with more aliasing on hard edges. The FSR 4.1 implementation is doing a lot of work here, and it looks great considering that it's rendering at 720p and getting upscaled up to 1080p. It's probably not the way that I will play the game over the coming weeks, but if that's what you have, GTA 6 is still an awesome game so far.

Now, I have about an hour played total on both my Xbox and PlayStation accounts, and obviously a lot can change over the course of this very long game. I'm going to keep at it, and hopefully GTA 6 continues to be a showcase of what these consoles are capable of at this point in their lifespan. And, at least at this point, I have no reason to suspect that it won't.
